The test image is a microscopic view showing branched fungal structures with dense grape-like clusters of spores at the tips (scale bar: 100µm). This is highly characteristic of Botrytis cinerea (Gray Mold) - the grape-like conidial clusters are its defining microscopic feature.

Let me view one reference image to confirm.

The reference image shows gray mold on a tomato (macroscopic view). The test image is clearly a microscopic view of fungal spore structures.

The microscopic features in the test image are definitive:
- Branched conidiophores with dense, grape-like clusters of oval conidia at the tips
- This is the textbook microscopic signature of *Botrytis cinerea* — the name "Botrytis" literally derives from Greek for "grape cluster"
- Scale is 100µm, consistent with Botrytis conidia size (~10-15µm)

No other class in this list matches: Rhizopus would show round sporangia on unbranched stalks; Powdery Mildew would show chains of oidia; Alternaria would have larger multi-septate conidia.
